chunks: 1- Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Sahl from Adam ibn Ali from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:
Whoever performs Hajj on behalf of a person who does not have the wealth to perform it, it suffices for him until God grants him the means to perform it and Hajj becomes obligatory upon him.

2- Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad, all of them, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
If a poor man were performed Hajj on his behalf by another man, it would count as one Hajj for him; and when he becomes wealthy afterwards, Hajj becomes obligatory upon him.
3- As for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who performed Hajj on behalf of another; does that suffice for him for the Hajj of Islam? He said: Yes. I said: Is the Hajj of the wealthy person complete or incomplete? He said: Complete. I said: Is the Hajj of the poor person complete or incomplete? He said: Complete.

So it does not contradict the first two narrations, because his saying 'it suffices for him for the Hajj of Islam' refers to the Hajj that is recommended in the state of poverty, not the one that is obligatory upon him in the state of wealth, because that latter one can be expressed as the Hajj of Islam as we have clarified.

key_terms.حَجَّةُ الْأَجِيرِ: The Hajj of the poor person (one who is in need)
key_terms.حَجَّةُ الْإِسْلَامِ: Hajj of Islam (referring to the recommended or obligatory Hajj depending on context)
key_terms.حَجَّةُ الْجَمَّالِ: The Hajj of the wealthy person (one who has sufficient means)

ai.seo_question: Does performing Hajj on behalf of a poor person count towards their obligatory Hajj if they later become wealthy?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi synthesizes these narrations to clarify the distinction between the 'Hajj of Islam' (recommended) and the obligatory Hajj, noting that a proxy's performance suffices for the poor until they gain the means. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that financial capacity is a condition for the obligation (wujub) of Hajj, not its validity, allowing the poor to fulfill their duty through delegation. The text resolves apparent contradictions by distinguishing between the recommended act performed during poverty and the mandatory act that becomes due upon wealth.
